lines.text: “We need the flashlight now,” said Jack.
Annie took it off her belt and switched it on.
Step by step, she and Jack walked between the trees.
said Annie, shining the flashlight in Jack’s face.
Annie shined her flashlight over the tops of the trees.
At the top of the tallest tree in the woods.
Annie shined her light at the tree house, and then down the tall ladder.
All the way to the ground.
She gripped the flashlight and began to climb.
What if someone was in the tree house?
Jack was alone in the dark.
Then he thought about all the books in the tree house.
When he was nearly to the tree house, he saw light in the distant sky.
He crawled through a hole in the floor and took off his backpack.
It was dark inside the tree house.
Annie was shining her flashlight on the books scattered about.
She stopped the light on a dinosaur book.
It was the book that had taken them to the time of the dinosaurs.
How could anyone forget seeing a real live Tyrannosaurus rex?
The light fell on a book about Pennsylvania.
A red silk bookmark stuck out of it.
That was the picture that had brought them home.
The light was shining on a book about knights and castles.
There was a blue leather bookmark in it.
Annie turned to the page with the bookmark.
There was a picture of a knight on a black horse.
He was riding toward a castle.
“We wish we could see this guy for real,” Annie said.
It sounded like a horse neighing.
They both went to the window.
Annie shined the flashlight down on the ground.
Then the wind began to moan.
And the tree house started to spin.
The air was damp and cool.
The sound of a horse’s whinny came again from below.
She was still holding the castle book.
A huge castle loomed out of the fog.
The tree house was in a different oak tree.
And down below, the knight on the black horse was riding by.
“We have to go home and make a plan first.”
He picked up the book about Pennsylvania.
He opened it to the page with the red silk bookmark.
He pointed to the photograph of the Frog Creek woods.
She yanked the book away from him.
I want to visit the castle!”
We have to examine the situation,” said Jack.
She clipped the flashlight to her belt.
And she scooted down the ladder.
Besides, he sort of wanted to take a peek himself.
He put down the book about Pennsylvania.
He dropped the castle book into his pack.
And headed down into the cool, misty air.
Annie was under the tree, looking across the foggy ground.
“The knight’s riding toward that bridge, I think,” said Annie.
I’ll look it up,” said Jack.
He took the flashlight from her and pulled the castle book out of his pack.
He opened it to the page with the leather bookmark.
He read the words under the picture of the knight: This is a knight arriving for a castle feast.
Knights wore armor when they traveled long and dangerous distances.
A helmet alone could weigh up to forty pounds.
Jack had weighed forty pounds when he was five years old.
So it’d be like riding a horse with a fiveyear-old on your head.
He wanted to take notes, as he’d done on their dinosaur trip.
He turned the pages of the castle book.
He found a picture that showed the whole castle and the buildings around it.
“The knight’s crossing the bridge,” said Annie.
“He’s going through the gate .… He’s gone.”
Jack studied the bridge in the picture.
He read: A drawbridge crossed the moat.
The moat was filled with water, to help protect the castle from enemies.
Some people believe crocodiles were kept in the moat.
said Annie, peering through the mist.
“Yeah, there’s a windmill in here, too,” said Jack, pointing at the picture.
“Look at the real one, Jack,” said Annie.
A piercing shriek split the air.
“It sounded like it came from that little house over there!”
“There’s a little house here,” said Jack, studying the picture.
He turned the page and read: The hawk house was in the inner ward of the castle.
Hawks were trained to hunt other birds and small animals.
Jack wrote in his notebook: “We must be in the inner ward,” said Jack.
He turned more pages of the book.
“I want to see what’s really going on, Jack.
Not what’s in the book,” said Annie.
He pointed to a picture of a big party.
Men were standing by the door, playing drums and horns.
He read: Fanfares were played to announce different dishes in a feast.
Feasts were held in the Great Hall.
I’m going to the real feast,” said Annie.
It showed boys his age carrying trays of food.
Jack wrote: He held up the book to show Annie.
“Look, I think they eat—” Where was she?
He heard the real drums and the real horns.
He saw the real hawk house, the real windmill, the real moat.
He saw Annie dashing across the real drawbridge.
Then she vanished through the gate leading to the castle.
“I’m going to kill her,” muttered Jack.
He threw his stuff into his pack and moved toward the drawbridge.
He hoped no one would see him.
When he got to the bridge, he started across.
The wooden planks creaked under his feet.
He peered over the edge of the bridge.
Were there any crocodiles in the moat?
A guard on top of the castle wall was looking down.
He ran through the castle gate and into the courtyard.
From inside the castle came the sounds of music, shouting, and laughter.
Jack hurried to a dark corner and crouched down.
He shivered as he looked around for Annie.
Torches lit the high wall around the courtyard.
Two boys led horses that clopped over the gray cobblestones.
It was the knight’s black horse!
She was hiding behind a well in the center of the courtyard.
He waited till the boys and horses disappeared inside the stable.
Then he dashed to the well.
They tiptoed together across the cobblestones.
Then they slipped into the entrance of the castle.
Noise and music came from a bright room in front of them.
They stood on one side of the doorway and peeked in.
He held his breath as he stared in awe.
A giant fireplace blazed at one end of the noisy room.
Antlers and rugs hung on the stone walls.
Boys in short dresses carried huge trays of food.
Dogs were fighting over bones under the tables.
People in bright clothes and funny hats strolled among the crowd.
Some tossed balls in the air.
Some balanced swords on their hands.
Men and women dressed in capes and furs sat at long, crowded wooden tables.
“I wonder which one is the knight,” said Jack.
A man carrying a tray of pies was standing a few feet away.
Then they ran as fast as they could down a dimly lit hallway.
Annie dashed toward a door off the hallway.
The two of them stumbled into a dark, cold room.
The door creaked shut behind them.
Jack handed it to her, and she switched it on.
A row of knights right in front of them!
Annie turned the light back on.
“Let me have the flashlight a second,” said Jack.
“So I can look in the book.”
He pulled out the castle book.
He flipped through the pages until he found what he was looking for.
“It’s where armor and weapons are stored.”
He shined the flashlight around the room.
The light fell on shiny breastplates, leg plates, arm plates.
On shelves filled with helmets and weapons.
On shields, spears, swords, crossbows, clubs, battle-axes.
There was a noise in the hall.
“I’ve got to check on something first.”
“It’ll take just a second,” said Jack.
He tried to lift a helmet from a shelf.
He bent over and dragged the helmet over his head.
It was worse than having a five-year-old on your head.
More like having a ten-year-old on your head.
Not only could Jack not lift his head, he couldn’t see anything, either.
Jack’s voice echoed inside the metal chamber.
He struggled to get the helmet off.
Suddenly he lost his balance and went crashing into other pieces of armor.
The metal plates and weapons clattered to the floor.
Jack lay on the floor in the dark.
But his head was too heavy.
Someone grabbed him by the arm.
The next thing he knew, his helmet was yanked off.
He was staring into the blazing light of a fiery torch.
In the torchlight, Jack saw three huge men standing over him.
One with very squinty eyes held the torch.
One with a very red face held Jack.
And one with a very long mustache held on to Annie.
said the one with the very long mustache.
said the one with the very red face.
The guards marched Jack and Annie out of the armory.
said a guard, giving him a push.
Down they marched, down the long, dark hallway.
Squinty, Annie, Mustache, Jack, and Red.
Jack heard Annie shouting at the guards.
They didn’t take her seriously at all.
At the bottom of the stairs was a big iron door with a bar across it.
Squinty pushed the bar off the door.
Then he shoved at the door.
Jack and Annie were pushed into a cold, clammy room.
The fiery torch lit the dungeon.
There were chains hanging from the filthy walls.
Water dripped from the ceiling, making puddles on the stone floor.
It was the creepiest place Jack had ever seen.
“We’ll keep them here till the feast is done.
Then turn them over to the Duke,” said Squinty.
“He knows how to take care of thieves.”
“There will be a hanging tomorrow,” said Mustache.
“If the rats don’t get them first,” said Red.
Jack saw that Annie had his backpack.
“Come on, let’s chain the two of ’em,” said Squinty.
Annie whipped her flashlight out of the pack.
They stared at the shiny flashlight in her hand.
They jumped back against the wall.
It fell into a dirty puddle on the floor, sputtered, and went out.
Annie fiercely pointed her light at one, then the other.
Each howled and covered his face.
One by one, the guards lay down on the wet floor.
Jack looked at the open doorway.
He looked at the guards quaking on the ground.
In one quick leap, Jack followed her out of the terrible dungeon.
Annie and Jack raced back up the winding stairs and down the long hallway.
They hadn’t gone far when they heard shouting behind them.
He shoved open a door off the hallway and pulled Annie into a dark room.
Then Annie shined her flashlight around the room.
There were rows of sacks and wooden barrels.
“I’d better look in the book,” said Jack.
Annie gave him the flashlight and his backpack.
He pulled out the book and started tearing through it.
Jack and Annie jumped behind the door as it creaked open.
A light from a torch danced wildly over the sacks and barrels.
His hands were trembling as he flipped through the pages of the castle book.
“Here’s a map of the castle,” he said.
“Look, this must be the room we’re in.
Jack studied the room in the book.
“These are sacks of flour and barrels of wine.”
He read aloud: This door leads from the storeroom through a secret passage to a precipice over the moat.
“But first we have to find the door.”
Jack looked at the picture carefully.
Then he shined the flashlight around the room.
The floor of the room was made up of stones.
The trapdoor in the picture was five stones away from the door to the hall.
Jack shined the light on the floor and counted the stones.
He stamped on the fifth stone.
He put the flashlight on the floor.
He worked his fingers under the thin sheet of stone and tried to lift it.
Annie came over and helped him lift the stone square out of its place.
Underneath was a small wooden door.
Jack and Annie tugged on the rope handle of the door.
The door fell open with a thunk.
Jack picked up the flashlight and shined it on the hole.
He clipped on the flashlight and felt his way down the small ladder.
When they both reached the bottom of the ladder, Jack shined the light around them.
He crouched down and began moving through the damp, creepy tunnel.
The flashlight barely lit the stone walls.
The light got dimmer and dimmer.
He was desperate to get out of the castle before the batteries died completely.
Soon he reached another small wooden door.
The door at the end of the tunnel!
Jack unlatched the door and pushed it open.
He couldn’t see anything in the misty darkness.
But I think we’ve come to the outside of the castle,” said Jack.
Jack put the flashlight in his pack.
He put the pack on his back.
He stuck his hand out the door.
“I’m going to have to go feet first,” he said.
Jack turned around in the small tunnel.
He lay down on his stomach.
He stuck one leg out the door.
Jack inched down, bit by bit.
Until he was hanging out the door, clinging to the ledge.
Water filled Jack’s nose and covered his head.
He grabbed them just in time.
He coughed and flailed his arms.
He tried to tread water and put his glasses back on.
With his backpack, his shoes, and his heavy clothes, he could hardly stay afloat.
Jack dog-paddled through the cold black water.
At first it seemed as if she was swimming in front of him.
But then he heard a splash behind him.
Her voice came from in front.
He couldn’t see anything through his water-streaked glasses.
Jack swam through the dark toward her voice.
He imagined a crocodile slithering after him.
Jack’s hand touched a wet, live thing.
She pulled him to the edge of the moat.
They crawled over an embankment onto the wet grass.
Another splash came from the moat waters.
He shook the water off his glasses and put them back on.
It was so misty he couldn’t see the castle.
He couldn’t even see the moat, much less a crocodile.
He peered at the foggy darkness.
Everything had been swallowed up by the thick, soupy darkness.
Jack reached into his wet backpack and pulled out the flashlight.
But in the still, cold darkness.
A full moon was shining in the sky.
A pool of light spread through the mist.
Then Jack and Annie saw him just a few feet away.
He sat on the black horse.
His armor shone in the moonlight.
But he seemed to be staring straight at Jack and Annie.
The knight held out his gloved hand.
“He wants to help us,” said Annie.
The knight picked Annie up and put her on the back of his horse.
Jack moved slowly toward the knight.
The knight picked him up, too.
He placed Jack on the horse, behind Annie.
The knight got on behind them.
The black horse cantered beside the moonlit water of the moat.
Jack rocked back and forth in the saddle.
He felt very brave and very powerful.
He felt as if he could ride forever on this horse, with this mysterious knight.
A hawk shrieked in the darkness.
She pointed toward a grove of trees.
The knight steered the horse toward the trees.
There it is,” Annie said, pointing to the ladder.
The knight brought his horse to a stop.
He dismounted and helped Annie down.
The knight got back on his horse.
Then he slapped the reins and rode off through the mist.
Annie started up the tall ladder, and Jack followed.
They climbed into the dark tree house and looked out the window.
The knight was riding toward the outer wall.
They saw him go through the outer gate.
Clouds started to cover the moon again.
For a brief moment, Jack thought he saw the knight’s armor gleaming on the top of a hill beyond the castle.
The clouds covered the moon completely.
And a black mist swallowed the land.
Jack shivered in his wet clothes as he kept staring at the blackness.
Jack heard Annie fumble in the darkness.
He kept looking out the window.
“I think this is it,” said Annie.
He was hoping to see the knight’s armor gleam again in the distance.
I’m going to use this,” said Annie.
“Because I think it’s the right one.
I wish we could go to Frog Creek!”
Jack heard the wind begin to blow.
“I hope I pointed to the right picture in the right book,” said Annie.
The tree house began to rock.
The wind got louder and louder.
“I hope it wasn’t the dinosaur book!”
Jack shouted at the tree house.
The tree house started to spin.
They both looked out the tree house window.
In the distance, streetlights lit their street.
There was a light on in their upstairs window.
“I think Mom and Dad are up.
In a daze, Jack unzipped his backpack.
He pulled out the castle book.
But Jack placed it back with all the other books.
said Annie, scooting out of the tree house.
Jack followed her down the ladder.
They reached the ground and took off between the gray-black trees.
They left the woods and ran down their deserted street.
They got to their yard and crept across the lawn.
Right up to the back door.
Jack and Annie slipped inside the house.
He led the way up the stairs and down the hall.
No sign of his mom or dad.
But he could hear water running in the bathroom.
Their house was so different from the dark, cold castle.
So safe and cozy and friendly.
Annie stopped at her bedroom door.
She gave Jack a smile, then disappeared inside her room.
He took off his damp clothes and pulled on his dry, soft pajamas.
He sat down on his bed and unzipped his backpack.
He took out his wet notebook.
He felt around for the pencil, but his hand touched something else.
Jack pulled the blue leather bookmark out of his pack.
It must have fallen out of the castle book.
Jack held the bookmark close to his lamp and studied it.
The leather was smooth and worn.
For the first time Jack noticed a letter on the bookmark.
Jack opened the drawer next to his bed.
He took out the gold medallion.
He looked at the letter on it.
Now this was an amazing new fact.
The person who had dropped the gold medallion in the time of the dinosaurs was the same person who owned all the books in the tree house.
Jack placed the bookmark next to the medallion.
He turned to the least wet page in his notebook.
And he started to write down this new fact.
But before he could draw the M, his eyes closed.
He dreamed they were with the knight again.
All three of them riding the black horse through the cool, dark night.
Beyond the outer wall of the castle.
And up over a moonlit hill.
